related_questions.question: When did student loan forgiveness start?

text_blocks.snippet: The concept of student loan forgiveness in the US, specifically through the Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) program, was established in 2007. This program, part of the College Cost Reduction and Access Act, aims to forgive remaining loan balances for borrowers who work full-time in public service and make 120 qualifying monthly payments. While the program was created in 2007, the first loan forgiveness under PSLF wasn't possible until after October 1, 2017.

list.snippet: The PSLF program was established by the College Cost Reduction and Access Act, signed into law by President George W. Bush.

list.title: Early 2017:
list.snippet: The earliest borrowers could begin receiving forgiveness under PSLF was October 1, 2017, after making 10 years of qualifying payments while working in public service.
President Joe Biden announced broader changes to student loan forgiveness, including a plan for $10,000 in relief for many borrowers and an additional $10,000 for Pell Grant recipients.

related_questions.question: Why did I get a student loan refund check?

text_blocks.snippet: You might receive a student loan refund check because your student loan disbursement exceeded your school's charges, or you made payments during the payment pause and requested a refund. These refunds can also occur due to adjustments in your payment count towards income-driven repayment plans or Public Service Loan Forgiveness, potentially resulting in a refund for overpayments.

list.snippet: When you borrow student loans, the funds are typically disbursed to your school, and any leftover amount after tuition and other fees are covered is considered a credit balance.
If this credit balance is not used for other qualified educational expenses, your school is required to refund it to you.
This refund can be in the form of a check or direct deposit.
During the payment pause on federal student loans (March 2020 to September 2023), many borrowers continued making payments.

The government allowed borrowers to request refunds for payments made during this period, especially if those payments brought the loan balance below certain forgiveness thresholds, according to CountyOffice.org.
These refunds were for payments made voluntarily, and the refunded amount might have been added back to your loan balance along with accrued interest.

text_blocks.snippet: 3. Adjustments to Payment Counts for Income-Driven Repayment (IDR) or PSLF:

list.snippet: The Department of Education (ED) adjusted payment counts for IDR and PSLF, potentially forgiving some borrowers' loans and leading to refunds for overpayments.
If you reached the forgiveness threshold (20 or 25 years for IDR, or qualifying payments under PSLF) with the adjusted count, you might have received a refund for any extra payments made.

list.title: Borrower Defense Discharge:
list.snippet: If you successfully applied for borrower defense discharge (claiming your school misled you), any payments made could be refunded.

list.title: Overpayments:
list.snippet: If you accidentally overpaid your loan, either through a manual payment or an over-disbursement of your loan, you may receive a refund.
Refunds from loan forgiveness programs (like PSLF) are generally not taxable.
Refunds for voluntary payments made during the payment pause might need to be paid back, as they are effectively reversing the benefit of those payments.
Always review your loan statements and communications from your loan servicer to understand the reason for the refund.
If you have any questions about a student loan refund, contact your loan servicer or the school that disbursed the loan.
